prompt:
69-year-old man with hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia, on lisinopril and tamsulosin, had a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL six months ago. He has three weeks of fatigue, migratory arthralgias, low-grade fevers, 4 kg weight loss, and nasal congestion with bloody crusting; he started ibuprofen for his joints. Creatinine today is 3.6. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein, and the lab reports dysmorphic red cells; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 1.8 g/g. BP is 158/92 and SpO2 97% with no hemoptysis. Urology suggested a CT urogram with contrast and cystoscopy for the hematuria. What would you do?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Recognize a likely rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis requiring urgent evaluation.
Obtain same-day nephrology consultation.
Send ANCA testing for MPO and PR3 antibodies.
Send anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies.
Arrange a kidney biopsy.
Stop ibuprofen.
Have an experienced reviewer examine the urine sediment for red cell casts.
Check complement C3 and C4.
Obtain a renal ultrasound.
Obtain chest imaging to assess for pulmonary involvement.
Start high-dose glucocorticoids without awaiting biopsy if serologies are positive or kidney function is declining rapidly.
Monitor for alveolar hemorrhage symptoms and follow the hemoglobin.
Check CBC and a metabolic panel, including potassium and bicarbonate, with serial creatinine.
Monitor urine output and watch for dialysis indications.
Start plasma exchange if anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are positive.
Send ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies.
Obtain hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV serologies.
Hold lisinopril during the acute kidney injury.
Refer to ENT to evaluate the sinonasal disease.
Send serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains.
Obtain blood cultures given fever, to exclude endocarditis-associated glomerulonephritis.
Adjust medication doses for renal function.
Order a CT urogram with intravenous contrast as the next step.
Attribute the kidney injury to NSAIDs and recheck in four weeks.
Refer for routine outpatient nephrology in two to three months.
Attribute the kidney injury to prostatic obstruction and increase tamsulosin without imaging.
Continue ibuprofen for the arthralgias.
Delay immunosuppression until biopsy when serologies are strongly positive and function is worsening.
Start cyclophosphamide empirically before serologies or biopsy.
Increase the lisinopril dose to control blood pressure and proteinuria now.
Give an intravenous fluid bolus for presumed prerenal injury.
Prescribe high-dose prednisone at home and follow up in one month.
Add spironolactone for blood pressure control.
Perform cystoscopy as the first evaluation of the hematuria.
Treat the sinus symptoms with antibiotics alone.
Order a 24-hour urine collection and defer serologies.
Order a PSA and prostate biopsy as the primary evaluation.
Diagnose vasculitis from ANCA alone and skip biopsy when it can be done safely.
